\chapter{The toolbox}\label{ch:toolbox}

Every reading in this part comes from one of a small set of tools. Each answers its own question and has its own specialty; together they look at a sample from different sides, so that what one cannot see another can. This chapter introduces each tool and says where it stands: \emph{commissioned} (it passed every test written for it before its data were read, and its readings in that scope are results), \emph{in development}, or a \emph{candidate} still being designed. The chapters that follow give the physics and the evidence.

\section{The instruments}

\subsection*{IAM-Atlas v2.1}
\textbf{The question.} What does each healthy cell look like, at every site, and how sure are we?\par
\textbf{How it reads.} A map of 79 kinds of healthy human cells, built from 21 public sources on arrays and sequencing, fitted as one model so every spot on the genome carries its value and its uncertainty. Like combining many sensors into one estimate, each weighted by how far it can be trusted.\par
\textbf{Its specialty.} It is the map every other instrument reads against: for 79 healthy cell types, the expected tagging at every site with its range of error, so a sample can be split into its cells and each cell compared with its own healthy kind. (Chapter~\ref{ch:atlas})\par
\textbf{Reads from.} arrays or sequencing. \textbf{Status.} Commissioned (79 cell types; met all three sealed bars against both published reference atlases; commissioned for three cell references and the colon and lung tissue tests).\par

\subsection*{IAM-Deconvolver}
\textbf{The question.} How much of each cell is in a mixed sample?\par
\textbf{How it reads.} Reads a mixed sample against IAM-Atlas v2.1 and reports each cell's share with its range, after a sample check that refuses arrays it cannot read. On 200 fresh mixtures from a laboratory the atlas never saw, the shares came back within 0.016 of the truth (mean absolute error). Read and flagged development: every one of the atlas's 79 cells in one run; nine known mixtures of tissue DNA in blood were found at the right size through the one command (mean error 0.0057, nothing that was not put in above 0.0030; `doors/data/DEV\_ONE\_DRAW\_01/run\_03/mixes\_03\_summary.txt`).\par
\textbf{Its specialty.} It turns a whole-blood array into its cells, so each instrument reads the cell it was built for and a change in the mix is not mistaken for a change in the cells. (Chapter~\ref{ch:atlas})\par
\textbf{Reads from.} arrays; sequencing values (development). \textbf{Status.} Commissioned (blood-cell shares on arrays, tested on neutrophils, monocytes, CD4 T and CD8 T cells).\par

\subsection*{Met-A}
\textbf{The question.} How far has a tissue's tagging level drifted toward the ceiling?\par
\textbf{How it reads.} Reads the methylation level at each cell's identity sites, sites a healthy cell holds mostly marked or mostly unmarked, steadily from one healthy sample to the next, chosen away from the ends so that wear can show; against IAM-Atlas v2.1, on cheap and plentiful arrays. Commissioned on isolated neutrophils. Each cell is read at its own identity sites, the sites it holds (where a loss can raise disorder) and healthy people agree on; reading every site is more sensitive but cannot say which cell is losing hold (DEV-EACH-CELL-01 exploration 4). Read and flagged development: Met-A for every cell the IAM-Deconvolver finds, each against its own profile in IAM-Atlas v2.1, on arrays and on sequencing values.\par
\textbf{Its specialty.} Cost and reach: a single array, the most common methylation measurement in the world, read on the gauge against the same cell type's healthy reference, with its detection limit printed. (Chapter~\ref{ch:meta})\par
\textbf{Reads from.} arrays. \textbf{Status.} Commissioned (tested and commissioned on isolated neutrophils, EPIC v1).\par

\subsection*{C-Score (the clustering meter)}
\textbf{The question.} Has the pattern started to clump?\par
\textbf{How it reads.} Cancer does not only shift tagging levels; it clumps them into runs. The C-Score measures that clumping, against the sample's own scattered change. Its first healthy limit was set on healthy arrays from many studies; Healthy comes only from the atlases, so it is being re-commissioned against IAM-Atlas v2.1 alone. Its limit will come from the atlases alone: each site's spread between healthy donors, how neighboring sites move together between donors, and the array's own noise.\par
\textbf{Its specialty.} The shape of a change, not its size: whether a sample's departures from healthy are scattered like ordinary wear or packed together in stretches, the way a tumor that silences or loses a region leaves them. It is the clustering step of the cosmic microwave background analysis chain, carried over to the genome. (Chapter~\ref{ch:cscore})\par
\textbf{Reads from.} arrays. \textbf{Status.} Commissioned (tested and commissioned on whole blood, EPIC v1).\par

\subsection*{IAM-A}
\textbf{The question.} Is each mark still held at its own healthy rate?\par
\textbf{How it reads.} Counts tagging mistakes one DNA molecule at a time, the most direct reading of informational fidelity we have, and reads them against the sample's own line. The physics end of the catalogue: the floor and ceiling are derived, and the healthy middle comes from the sample itself. Every reading states its own counting error: how many held-error chances it counted and the range that leaves.\par
\textbf{Its specialty.} That it reads single molecules and carries its own reference: how well each molecule held its marks, compared with the healthy level set by the cell's own loose share, with no library of other people's cells. (Chapter~\ref{ch:iama})\par
\textbf{Reads from.} single-molecule sequencing (bisulfite, EM-seq; nanopore next). \textbf{Status.} Commissioned (each sample against its own reference; sealed test on healthy blood CD8 T cells, whole-genome bisulfite).\par

\subsection*{Group-A}
\textbf{The question.} Has a whole group moved (a trial arm, an exposure, a cohort)?\par
\textbf{How it reads.} Single blood readings are too noisy for one person on arrays, but a group average is not. Group-A reads each person with the one command and compares the groups. It was first commissioned with each reading tared against healthy arrays run the same way; Healthy comes only from the atlases, so it is being re-commissioned against IAM-Atlas v2.1 alone. In that first commissioning, on 278 healthy people from a laboratory it had never read, women and men came out 0.36 \% apart, and a 1 \% loss planted into half of them was found at 7.253 standard errors.\par
\textbf{Its specialty.} Groups: whether a whole cohort, trial arm or exposure has moved, read as one, each person against the atlas. (Chapter~\ref{ch:groupa})\par
\textbf{Reads from.} arrays. \textbf{Status.} Commissioned (groups of whole bloods run in one series, EPIC v1).\par

\section{In development}

Readings the one command makes on every run, shown beside the commissioned ones and flagged as in development until each passes tests written before its data are read.

\subsection*{The IAM Sequencing Atlas}
A second atlas, for sequenced samples only, beside IAM-Atlas v2.1 (which stays the reference for arrays). Measured, not fitted: for each of 58 healthy cell types (megakaryocytes provisional), at every one of the 28.2 million CpGs of the hg19 numbering, it holds the donors and reads, the methylated reads, the healthy level, the spread between donors, each donor's own measured disorder, and two noise maps (sealed donor halves, and random halves of every donor's reads, which stand in where a cell has one donor). Each cell has reads at 97 to 98 \% of all CpGs, about 32 times the sites an array reads, so the sequencing instruments can read a sample's disorder at every CpG against healthy disorder of its own cell type. Built from the healthy sequencing inputs behind IAM-Atlas v2.1, with a granulocyte column added from three more donors, by the one command (run\_sample.py --build seq-atlas), every step checked first on constructed data with a known answer; it rebuilds from the public files in minutes. Each kind of instrument reads the same biology through its own chemistry. An array reads a probe's light, which never quite reaches 0 or 1: a site no cell ever marks still reads at the array's floor, a few percent up. Sequencing counts reads, so the same site reads about 0. Healthy disorder is computed from those levels, and near the floor a small offset in level is a large offset in disorder; the offset also changes with each laboratory's chemistry and library. So each kind of instrument reads against a ruler measured with its own chemistry: arrays against IAM-Atlas v2.1, sequenced samples against the IAM Sequencing Atlas. The physics and the instruments are the same; only the ruler changes with the platform. Read against IAM-Atlas v2.1, healthy sequenced samples showed it: at the islands every healthy cell keeps unmarked they read about 14 where healthy reads 1, and Met-A followed each sample's source. Read against it, the healthy inputs it was built from read sorted-cell Met-A 1.0075, whole-sample Met-A 1.0059, the islands 1.0118, the domains 1.0014, the C-Score 1.0003 (they built it, so this checks the build, not a new person). It carries the sky-survey tools a faint signal on a sphere needs: each cell drawn on the sphere with the range of its average, its two noise maps and their null tests, the genome-distance spectrum, masks for the sex chromosomes and poorly mapping sites, and an information sphere. Each library's floor, the rate of false "methylated" calls its chemistry adds, is measured at the sites no healthy cell marks. The whole atlas at every CpG, with its runtime tables and a checksum for every piece, is deposited on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24029328).\par
\textbf{Next.} Each cell commissioned on healthy sequenced samples from laboratories the atlas does not hold; columns for cells it lacks (megakaryocytes and later erythroid stages) as public data allows.\par

\subsection*{Array and Sequencing Information Spheres}
Method: each site placed on a sphere by its methylation profile across the healthy cell types, with each site's average level removed first, so sites that behave alike land together wherever they sit on the DNA; distances follow the Fisher-Rao metric of information geometry. The Array Information Sphere holds 191,458 sites from IAM-Atlas v2.1's 79 cell types; the Sequencing Information Sphere 534,617 sites from 56 of the sequencing atlas's cell types (to be rebuilt with all 57). Tested on IAM-Atlas v2.1 against 1,000 level-matched random groups: 11 of 12 cell-marker groups land together beyond what their level alone gives; 0 of 100 look-alike groups of the same levels pass, so it does not invent groups; distance agreement 0.8065. Adds: a globe shows where on the genome a change is; an information sphere shows whether the changed sites belong to one cell program spread over many chromosomes.\par
\textbf{Next.} The test on the real atlas with level-matched lines; then a person's information sphere against their own healthy one.\par

\subsection*{C-Score variants}
The C-Score reads how a change is laid out along the genome, not how large it is, against the sample's own spread, so a laboratory's offset cancels. Three versions: the commissioned one at Met-A's neutrophil sites; the whole-genome version on the globe's change map against IAM-Atlas v2.1; and IAM-A's, the clustering of held-error departures along the genome on single molecules.\par
\textbf{Next.} Each version read on healthy samples first, then on tumors.\par

\subsection*{Per-cell readings in a mixed sample}
One run of the one command finds every cell of IAM-Atlas v2.1 in a sample and reads Met-A for each, against its own healthy profile; each cell also gets its own change layer on the globe. Each row states how much of its reading is the cell's own: a cell's reading at its identity sites also carries the DNA of the cells around it, in proportion to the DNA each holds there. Sites held by one cell alone are the next test, so a loss across a cell's whole pattern can be put on the right cell.\par
\textbf{Next.} Each cell's reading divided by its own healthy prediction, and each cell's healthy width measured from the atlas's own donors.\par

\subsection*{Buffy coat and plasma from one draw}
One tube, two halves: the buffy coat (the person's own white cells, long DNA) and the plasma (cell-free DNA). The one command reads both and writes one record, including what the plasma holds that the person's own white cells do not explain, and IAM-Atlas v2.1 says which tissue it came from. Constructed draws with known answers test it; a public set of matched halves from healthy people is held unread for the test that counts. Plasma is read against the IAM Sequencing Atlas at about one read per site: Met-A at the identity sites of the cells found reads 0.9918 on healthy plasma, and the islands carry each library's floor, read 0.9272 at a common floor. Constructed healthy plasmas read Normal at 20 reads per site, so the instrument's own reach is known by depth.\par
\textbf{Next.} What the plasma DNA the Deconvolver gives to erythroid cells is; then the held set of matched halves.\par

\subsection*{Island and domain readings}
Two fixed sets of sites the identity readings do not reach, each read on the A-score gauge against the atlas of the sample's own platform (IAM-Atlas v2.1 for arrays, the IAM Sequencing Atlas for sequencing) at each site's own read count: the islands, sites every healthy cell type keeps unmarked, where a mark gained is disorder; and the domains, marked sites some healthy cell types hold loosely, where the hold is lost first. Every run of the one command reads both, on arrays and on sequencing, so a change outside a cell's identity sites is seen where it starts. The synthetic tests pass, and tumors read above their own normal tissue on the islands. On sequencing the islands' expectation is counted from the reference's own reads; healthy sequenced inputs read the islands 1.0118 and the domains 1.0014. The idea came from the information-theory study of pediatric leukemia (Nature Biomedical Engineering, 2021, doi:10.1038/s41551-021-00703-2); IAM adds the reading of both places in one sample, against the atlas in that person's own cell mix, on a gauge whose ends are fixed by physics.\par
\textbf{Next.} Tumors and blood cancers against their own healthy cells, on arrays and on sequencing.\par

\subsection*{Nearest-neighbor coupling (Coupling-A)}
Whether a molecule's held errors fall one at a time or together, read on the A-score gauge as coupling-A: the sample's coupling (neighboring CpGs that lost their mark together on held molecules, over what each molecule's own length and error count give at random) over the healthy coupling of its own cell type, so a healthy cell reads 1. The gauge's ends are counted: 0 when no two errors are ever neighbors, and the sample's own most clustered arrangement, every molecule's errors in one run. Its healthy reference comes from the 153 healthy sequencing samples behind IAM-Atlas v2.1, 56 cell types: errors cluster in every healthy cell, more in some, and read against its own cell type a healthy sample sits within 0.935 to 1.062. It asks a question from the information-theory study of methylation: is a mark kept site by site, or by a stretch of DNA as a unit? Every sequencing report draws it. The idea came from the information-theory study of pediatric leukemia (Nature Biomedical Engineering, 2021, doi:10.1038/s41551-021-00703-2); IAM adds the gauge, one sample against its own cell type's healthy coupling between counted ends.\par
\textbf{Next.} Healthy sorted B and T cells from laboratories the atlas has never held, read against the IAM Sequencing Atlas once the sequencing chain is working; then the first question, written before it is read: does switching off the maintenance machinery change how the errors cluster?\par

\subsection*{Met-A on sequencing}
Met-A for a sample sequenced by whole-genome bisulfite, read against the IAM Sequencing Atlas, the ruler measured with sequencing's own chemistry. A sorted cell is read donor by donor: the sample's disorder at its cell's identity sites against that of each healthy donor of the same cell, both at the same number of reads, so counting is exact on both sides and nothing is fitted. A mixed sample is read against the atlas in its own cell shares.\par
\textbf{Next.} After the array instruments are commissioned: the sequencing chain working (each library's own false-call floor at the islands, and copies in amplified libraries), then samples from other laboratories read against the IAM Sequencing Atlas alone.\par

\subsection*{Genome-coverage check}
Before a sequenced sample is read, the chain checks that its reads cover every chromosome evenly, and refuses, naming the missing chromosomes, a sample read only in part. A thin library, thin on every chromosome alike, passes. Its synthetic met every case.\par
\textbf{Next.} commissioned with the next fresh sequencing test\par

\subsection*{Distance to maximum disorder}
How far a sample sits from the most disordered state its own cell type can reach, the ceiling the law sets for each cell, on the same gauge as every reading. Read and flagged on every run; on sequencing its counted ceiling met its synthetic.\par
\textbf{Next.} cancer researchers set where the lines fall on the gauge; commissioning on tumor and normal pairs from one laboratory\par

\subsection*{Sample Globe}
Method: every site of the sample against the person's own expected healthy profile (each atlas cell's healthy level, mixed at the sample's own cell shares), in units of that site's healthy range; a block of 10 neighboring sites counts as changed only beyond a 5 \% family-wise line, drawn on the atlas globe for its platform. Tested on sequencing: constructed healthy samples showed 2, 1 and 2 changed blocks (limit 50) and a planted change lit 231 of its 275 blocks (needed 139.5); on 35 outside healthy samples, pancreas reads level with the array version (156 against 158 changed blocks), while cortical neurons read 109 against 24, so the change count stays flagged. Adds: where on the genome a change sits, and whether it is clustered or scattered.\par
\textbf{Next.} its commissioning plan is written: healthy samples stay dark, planted changes light where planted\par

\subsection*{Serial samples from one person}
Two or more draws of the same person, read the same way: the later against the earlier, at every site both measured, so the person is their own reference.\par
\textbf{Next.} the tools are being moved onto the current chain's records; public data with repeated draws of the same healthy people is held for its test\par

\subsection*{Same-laboratory reference correction (sequencing)}
Retired: healthy comes only from the atlases. A few healthy samples of the same cell from the same laboratory set that laboratory's level, and every other sample from it is read against them. On two outside laboratories, three of their own healthy samples brought them to Normal.\par
\textbf{Next.} the test on a laboratory never read before is running\par

\section{The tools the instruments run on}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Intake and calibration.} Takes an array's raw intensities, checks every control, and turns them into tagging levels on one fixed scale, refusing what it cannot read and saying why. (Chapter~\ref{ch:instrument})
\item \textbf{Same-run reference correction.} Reads each specimen against healthy references run beside it, so a laboratory's own offset cancels instead of passing for disease. (Chapter~\ref{ch:instrument})
\item \textbf{Composition.} For whole blood, works out which cells are in the sample and in what shares, so a change in the mix is not mistaken for a change in the cells. (Chapter~\ref{ch:chain})
\item \textbf{Pipeline run and report.} Runs every stage in a fixed order, records every input and setting, and prints one report per sample with each instrument's reading, its status and its detection limit. (Chapter~\ref{ch:report})
\item \textbf{Array and Sequencing Atlas Globes, and the Globe Viewer.} Method: each atlas's sites placed on an equal-area HEALPix sphere (NSIDE 256, nested ordering) in genome order, each pixel holding a cell's methylation level and its 95 \% range: the Array Atlas Globe (IAM-Atlas v2.1, 813,951 array sites) and the Sequencing Atlas Globe (the IAM Sequencing Atlas on the same 813,951-site layout; the atlas itself holds every one of the 28.2 million CpGs, and its globe at every CpG is built and published: all 28,217,448 CpGs at NSIDE 2048, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.24029332). Tested: on the Sequencing Atlas Globe the stated 95 \% ranges match the true spread (stated over true variance 1.010 with two donors, 1.007 with three; coverage 0.955 and 0.948); a read-half noise map sits inside its shuffled null in all 56 cells, and a donor-half noise map shows where healthy people differ from one another. Adds: every site of every cell in one fixed place, so a cell, a sample and the uncertainty can be compared pixel for pixel, with the spectrum, mask and null methods built for all-sky maps. The Globe Viewer shows both atlases, every cell of each (79 and 57), and example readings. (Chapter~\ref{ch:sky})
\end{itemize}

\section{Candidates}

Readings still being designed, each with what it would add and what it cannot see. A candidate becomes an instrument only by passing tests written before its data are read.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Territory contrast.} \emph{What it reads:} where the loss happens first; a sustained energy shortfall should take the late-replicating, solo-WCGW territory before it touches housekeeping promoters \emph{What it adds:} self-taring; a ratio inside one array, so plate, batch and much of the composition effect cancel because numerator and denominator see the same cell mixture. It addresses the laboratory-to-laboratory spread that limits single whole-blood readings \emph{What it cannot see:} says nothing about absolute fidelity; a loss uniform across territories is invisible (confirmed, 0.1 \% of the signal). And the practical failure: a difference cancels an additive plate offset exactly but cannot cancel a multiplicative one; a 10 \% composition change moves it about 5x what a 2 \% shortfall does; while the beta = 1 ceiling makes offsets and noise one-sided
\item \textbf{Met-A on whole blood.} \emph{What it reads:} total disorder above what the estimated cell mixture explains; the existing composition-aware reading, in a tube of blood \emph{What it adds:} group comparisons are within reach now: with 50 people a mean loss of about 0.27 \% separates the group from healthy, and the function already exists in the chain \emph{What it cannot see:} an array averages molecules before anyone reads them, so one cell type can never be isolated. Across laboratories without a shared series the raw reading carries a 3.7 \% offset, which is inside the tumor range, so every comparison needs the same-series tare
\item \textbf{Distance to the ceiling.} \emph{What it reads:} how close a sample sits to the derived entropy ceiling; the right-hand mark of the gauge, past which the reading stops rising with further loss \emph{What it adds:} derived with no free parameter, and it answers how far from the ceiling a tumor arrives \emph{What it cannot see:} only informative for samples near the ceiling; says nothing about a healthy-range sample
\item \textbf{Run-length spectrum of losses.} \emph{What it reads:} the shape of clustering; exponential against heavy-tailed, which separates a processive mechanism from independent point losses \emph{What it adds:} same data as the clustering meter, different question; distinguishes mechanism rather than only size \emph{What it cannot see:} impossible on arrays; needs depth, so shallow libraries are out
\item \textbf{Tail of fragments in plasma (the early-detection instrument).} \emph{What it reads:} the few badly disordered molecules in a plasma sample, not the average; because early cancer is a tiny minority of fragments and an average hides it by construction \emph{What it adds:} the highest reward on the whole board; it is the blood test, and a tail statistic is the right shape for early detection \emph{What it cannot see:} needs depth and fragment length; a shallow or heavily fragmented sample has no tail to read. Composition of plasma is itself a question
\end{itemize}

\section{Why several}

Each instrument answers a different question about the same sample, so together they leave no blind side. IAM-Atlas v2.1 is the healthy reference every reading uses. The IAM-Deconvolver says whose DNA it is: which cells are in the sample, and in what shares. Met-A says how far each of those cells has drifted toward the ceiling. The C-Score says whether the pattern has started to clump. IAM-A says whether each mark is still held at its own healthy rate. Group-A says whether a whole group has moved, for studies rather than single patients. Every reading is also drawn on the globe, where it sits on the genome, against its healthy reference. A tumor that hides from one reading still has to answer to the others.
